questions.q: Am I eligible to vote?
questions.a: You must be a US Citizen, you must be 18 years of age by the time of the election, you must have lived 30 days in your county and 10 days in your precinct, you are not imprisoned for a felony

questions.q: How do I register to vote?
questions.a: You can register online at VOTE.NV.Gov (https://registertovote.nv.gov/) , you can also print out an application online here (https://www.nvsos.gov/elections/voters/registering-to-vote) and mail it back to the county clerk or registrar of voters of the county where you live.

questions.q: What is same-day registration?
questions.a: Same-day registration allows a voter to register for the first time or update their existing registration on the same day they vote. You can find important details related to same day registration here (https://www.nvsos.gov/elections/election-information/same-day-registration).

questions.q: Can I vote early by mail?
questions.a: Yes, With the passage of Assembly Bill 321 (https://www.leg.state.nv.us/App/NELIS/REL/81st2021/Bill/7842/Text) during the 2021 Legislative Session, all registered voters will receive a ballot by mail. You can request to opt-out by submitting this form [English (https://www.nvsos.gov/home/showpublisheddocument/16986/639082387841370000)] (https://www.nvsos.gov/home/showpublisheddocument/15882/638748891773370000), [Spanish] (https://www.nvsos.gov/home/showpublisheddocument/16988/639077832006970000), or [Filipino] (https://www.nvsos.gov/home/showpublisheddocument/16990/639077831589970000) to your county clerk.

questions.q: When is early voting in-person?
questions.a: Early voting for the 2026 Primary Election is May 23, 2026 - June 5, 2026 / Early voting for the 2026 General Election is October 17, 2026 - October 30, 2026

questions.q: When is Election Day?
questions.a: 2026 Primary Election Day is June 9, 2026 and 2026 General Election Day is November 3, 2026

questions.q: Where do I go vote?
questions.a: Each county has a polling location. You can find yours here (https://www.nvsos.gov/elections/election-information/2026-election-information/2026-polling-locations).

questions.q: What is a Primary Election vs. a General Election?
questions.a: A primary election is when political parties choose their nominees for the general election. A general election is when voters choose who actually gets the office.

questions.q: What is a poll watcher or an observer?
questions.a:
Poll watchers or election observers are individuals who may observe steps in the election process. A poll watchers may be members of organizations such as a political party or nonpartisan group, candidate representative, international observers, exit polling groups, academics, or relevant federal and state agencies.

The role of a poll watcher is to observe and monitor the election, without violating voter privacy or disrupting the election. The link below is to the form individuals must acknowledge and sign prior to being allowed to observe in a polling location. This form outlines the process and what is prohibited acts by a poll watcher inside a polling location.

Polling Place Observer Acknowledgment NAC 293.245 (nvsos.gov) (https://www.nvsos.gov/home/showpublisheddocument/12483/638380746502070000)

questions.q: Who is running in this election?
questions.a: You can find a complete list of candidates that are running in the 2026 General Election here (https://www.nvsos.gov/home/showpublisheddocument/20105/639232733439300000).

questions.q: Why does it take 10-15 days after the election to show my final vote history?
questions.a: Election results are unofficial until they have been canvassed by the counties and certified by the State. State law allows correctly post-marked mail ballots to be received by the county clerk until 5pm on the fourth day after the election per NRS 293.317. After all in-person and mail ballots have been counted, the clerks count the provisional ballots. Once these remaining ballots have been counted, the clerks must certify their election results to their county commissioners and transmit the results to the Secretary of State by the 10th day following the election per NRS 293.387. The information is posted to www.NVSOS.gov/votersearch (http://www.nvsos.gov/votersearch) within 48 hours.

questions.q: Who is eligible to register to vote? What are the qualifications to register to vote in Nevada?
questions.a:
Nevada law has specific requirements you must follow before you are eligible to vote. Below are the specific requirements.

- Be at least 18 years of age on or before Election Day.
- Be a U.S. Citizen.
- Be a resident of Nevada for 30 days preceding any election.
- Not currently serving a term of imprisonment for a felony, and/or;
- Not have been declared mentally incompetent by a court of law.

Individuals who are 17 years old and meet all the other qualifications to register to vote can pre-register to vote using any of the means available. A person who has preregistered to vote automatically becomes a registered voter on their birthday, unless the preregistration has been cancelled.

questions.q: Can I register to vote online?
questions.a: Yes, you may register to vote online on our website here (https://nvsos.gov/sosvoterservices/Registration/step1.aspx) with a valid Nevada Driver's License or Nevada ID.

questions.q: Where do I send my voter registration form once I’ve filled it out?
questions.a:
If you are registering to vote in Nevada, return your completed application via mail or in person at:

 • Your County Clerk/Registrar of Voters office;
  (https://www.nvsos.gov/elections/voters/county-clerk-contact-information) • Your City Clerk Office; or
  (https://www.nvsos.gov/elections/voters/city-clerk-contact-information) • Nevada Department of Motor Vehicles (http://www.dmvnv.com/)

questions.q: What happens after I submit my voter registration application?
questions.a:
When you application is received by the clerk/registrar, they will process and verify your voter registration application for accuracy, ensure your information matches with the Department of Motor Vehicles, Social Security Administration and Vital Statics. Once you are registered to vote in Nevada, you will receive a voter registration card by mail from your County Clerk/Registrar of Voters (https://www.nvsos.gov/elections/voters/county-clerk-contact-information) office, as well as a sample ballot prior to the Primary or General Elections. Sample ballots contain information on the offices up for election in your precinct and questions appearing on the actual ballot. They also contain information about your precinct, your party affiliation, the name and address of your polling place and early voting schedule and locations.

If you do not receive your voter registration card or sample ballot, please contact your local City (https://www.nvsos.gov/elections/voters/city-clerk-contact-information) Clerk or County Clerk/Registrar of Voters (https://www.nvsos.gov/elections/voters/county-clerk-contact-information) to verify that your application was received and processed.

questions.q: How can I confirm I am registered to vote or change my voter registration?
questions.a: You can view or update your voter registration information, please go to  (https://nvsos.gov/votersearch/)My Voter File (https://nvsos.gov/votersearch/).

questions.q: How do I cancel my voter registration?
questions.a: You can cancel your voter registration by visiting Voter Registration Search (nvsos.gov) (https://www.nvsos.gov/votersearch/) or you can submit a written request directly to the County Clerk/Registrar.

questions.q: Can I vote if I’ve been convicted of a crime?
questions.a: If you are not currently serving a term of imprisonment for a felony conviction, you are eligible to vote. For more about AB431 and the restoration of voting rights, click here (https://www.nvsos.gov/elections/voters/restoration-of-voting-rights-in-nevada).

questions.q: Do I declare my political party affiliation when I register to vote?
questions.a: Yes, when you register to vote, you will be asked to indicate your party affiliation. You also have the option to register as a Nonpartisan voter, meaning you have no political party affiliation. If you chose Nonpartisan or one of the minor parties, during a primary election you will only see on your ballot the offices that are nonpartisan.

questions.q: I didn’t vote in the last election; do I need to re-register?
questions.a: If you did not vote in the last election, and you did not return a postcard mailed to you pursuant to NRS 293.530 (http://www.leg.state.nv.us/nrs/NRS-293.html#NRS293Sec530), your voter registration will be put into inactive status. "Inactive Voter" status includes any voter for whom a county has received: 1) a returned residency confirmation mailing without a forwarding address within the same county, or 2) information obtained through the United States Postal Service National Change of Address (NCOA) database indicating that a voter has moved outside the county. An inactive voter is eligible to vote so long as they have met all other legal requirements to vote. If you do not vote in two consecutive federal elections, your local County Clerk/Registrar of Voters (https://www.nvsos.gov/elections/voters/county-clerk-contact-information) office must CANCEL your registration, pursuant to the National Voter Registration Act (NVRA). If your voter registration is cancelled, you must re-register to vote. You can check your voter information anytime online at My Voter File (https://www.nvsos.gov/SOSVoterServices/start.aspx).

questions.q: Can register to vote during Early Voting or on Election Day?
Can I use my tribal ID card to same-day register to vote?
I have not yet received my official Nevada Driver’s License or Nevada ID card in the mail; can I use the temporary, paper version to same-day register?
questions.a: Yes. The temporary paper driver’s license or ID card from the DMV is called an “interim document” and is a legitimate and verifiable piece of identification.

questions.q: I recently moved to Nevada and do not yet have a Nevada Driver’s License or Nevada ID card, can I same-day register?
questions.a: No. To same-day register you must have a valid Nevada driver’s license or ID card. There are no exceptions to this rule.

questions.q: Can I challenge someone’s voter registration?
questions.a:
A written challenge may be filed 30 days prior to election day and no later than 25 days prior to election day with the County Clerk/Registrar (May 11, 2026 – May 15, 2026). NRS 293.547(1) (https://www.leg.state.nv.us/nrs/nrs-293.html#NRS293Sec547)

Written Challenge Affirmation (nvsos.gov) (https://www.nvsos.gov/home/showpublisheddocument/16982/639017352849130000)

questions.q: What is a “Presidential Preference Primary”?
questions.a: It is a primary election wherein a voter indicates a preference for a particular candidate to be a major party’s nominee for the presidency. This is a non-binding election by State law; it is up to the major parties to decide how to allocate delegates. State parties award delegates according to the party’s system of delegate allocation and these delegates then vote to formally select a candidate as their presidential nominee at the party’s national convention. Presidential preference primaries are conducted by state and county election officials, while caucuses are conducted by the parties themselves. The Secretary of State's Office is not involved in the party run caucuses.

questions.q: When is Primary Election Day?
questions.a: The Primary Election is held on the 2nd Tuesday in June of each even-number years (NRS 293.175(1) (https://www.leg.state.nv.us/NRS/NRS-293.html#NRS293Sec175)). For 2026 it will be held on June 9, 2026.

questions.q: Is the State of Nevada a “Closed” or “Open” Primary state?
questions.a: The State of Nevada is a closed primary state. This means you must be registered to one of the major political parties to vote in that party’s primary election. For example, only voters who are registered to a major political party may vote for that respective parties’ candidates for nomination to appear on the general election ballot. There are a number of nonpartisan local and state offices that can also appear on a primary ballot. These races are open for all voters. An open primary is when a voter is not required to be affiliated with a political party in order to vote for partisan candidates.

questions.q: When is the last day I can register to vote for the upcoming Primary Election?
questions.a: The last day you can register to vote or update your voter information by mail or in person is Tuesday, May 12, 2026. After that date you can only register to vote or update your voter information online at Nevada Voter Registration (nv.gov) (https://registertovote.nv.gov/)

questions.q: When is early voting for the Primary Election?
questions.a: Early Voting starts on Saturday, May 23, 2026 and ends Friday, June 5, 2026.

questions.q: When is the last day I can register to vote or update my voter registration and receive a mail-in ballot?
questions.a: The last day County Clerks/Registrar will mail out ballots to voters that have registered to vote or updated their voter registration for the Primary Election is Tuesday, May 26, 2026.

questions.q: What is the last day a mail-in ballot can be received to be counted, that has a postmark of election day?
questions.a: For the Primary Election, the last day is Saturday, June 13, 2026, by 5:00 p.m.

questions.q: What is the last day I can cure my mail-in ballot if it has been challenged?
questions.a: The last day to cure a challenged mail-in ballot is Monday, June 15, 2026, by 5:00 p.m.

questions.q: What is the last day I can opt-out of receiving a mail-in ballot for the Primary Election?
questions.a: The last day to submit an opt-out request for the primary election is April 10, 2026, or 60 days prior to election day.

questions.q: When should I expect to receive my sample ballot in the mail for the Primary Election?
questions.a: Per NRS 293.565 (https://www.leg.state.nv.us/nrs/nrs-293.html#NRS293Sec565), 293C.530 (https://www.leg.state.nv.us/nrs/NRS-293C.html#NRS293CSec530), NAC 293.120 (https://www.leg.state.nv.us/nac/NAC-293.html#NAC293Sec120) and AB148(2025) (https://www.leg.state.nv.us/App/NELIS/REL/83rd2025/Bill/12074/Text) The deadline for sample ballots to be distributed before early voting begins with a date of May 10, 2026.

questions.q: When will mail-in ballots start to be mailed out?
questions.a: UOCAVA voters will start to receive their ballots 45 days before election day, April 24, 2026. Voters that are having their ballots mailed out of state they will be mailed 40 days before election day or April 30, 2026. All mail-in ballots will be mailed out no later than 20 days prior to election day, however we advise you contact your County Clerk/Registrar to confirm the date your mail-in ballot will be in the postal system.

questions.q: When will I be able to access NVEASE?
questions.a: This portal will be active 45 days prior to election day, which is Saturday, April 24, 2026, and will be closed on election day at 7:00 p.m. when the polls close.

questions.q: When is the last day for the Board of County Commissioners to canvass votes?
questions.a: For the Primary Election it is June 19, 2026

questions.q: When will the Supreme Court canvass the votes?
questions.a: For the General Election it is November 24, 2026.

questions.q: Why did I receive a ballot in the mail when I did not request one?
questions.a: That was caused by the passage of Assembly Bill 321 during the 2021 Legislative Session and now codified in NRS293.269911 (https://www.leg.state.nv.us/nrs/nrs-293.html#NRS293Sec269911). As a result, all active registered voters in Nevada will receive mail ballots. If you have not registered to vote 14 days prior to each election, you will not receive a mail-in ballot and will have to vote in person during early voting or on Election Day.

questions.q: I haven’t received my ballot in the mail, and it shows it was mailed, what should I do?
questions.a: If you have not received a ballot within a week of your ballot being mailed, please contact your County Clerk or Registrar of Voters.

questions.q: Do I have to use a stamp when I mail in my ballot? Do I have to mail it in?
questions.a: All ballots come with a secure pre-addressed, postage-paid ballot return envelope that must be used for returning the ballot. Once you sign the outside of the envelope on the signature line, you can simply drop that in the mail. You can also return it to your county Clerk/Registrar. When you go to drop it off, someone with the Clerk/Registrar’s office will verify the ballot is signed and sealed, and then will place it in a secure ballot box.

questions.q: I don’t trust the postal service; can I still vote using my mail-in ballot?
questions.a: Yes, you may fill it out and bring it to a secure drop-off location established by your county clerk/registrar. 2026 voting locations - Early Voting and Election Day Locations and Drop Off locations. (https://www.nvsos.gov/elections/election-information/2026-election-information/2026-polling-locations)

questions.q: Is there a difference between the mail-in ballot and an absentee ballot?
questions.a: No, they are the exact same form and are processed the exact same way. The term ‘Absentee Ballot’ was removed from our statutes by Assembly Bill 321 during the 2021 Legislative Session.

questions.q: What is the deadline to return my ballot?
questions.a: You can drop your mail ballot off at an official drop-box in your county or mail it in. If you choose to submit your ballot to a vote center, polling location or clerk/registrars office, it must be dropped off by 7:00pm on Election Day for it to be counted. Mail-in ballots that are postmarked on or before the day of the election AND received by the 4th day after election day by 5 p.m., will be accepted as received and processed according to Nevada State law. The Secretary of State's Office recommends mailing your ballot back at least one week before Election Day to ensure it arrives in a timely manner.

questions.q: What happens if I mail my ballot back the day after the election?
questions.a: If your mail-in ballot is received too late it will be received and challenged as “Too Late” and will not be processed.

questions.q: If I mail my ballot in, when will my vote be counted?
questions.a: Nevada counties can start processing votes cast through mail-in ballots 15 days before election day. However, the Board of County Commissioners & Carson City Board of Supervisors do not certify the election until “no later than the 10th day after Election Day”. That is when your vote will officially be considered “counted”.

questions.q: Is it possible to get two ballots in the mail?
questions.a: Yes, it is possible to get two ballots, but that does not mean someone can vote twice. If you misplace your ballot and request another from your county clerk/registrar, you will get a second ballot in the mail. If you then find your first ballot, you will have two ballots in-hand. However, the bar code on the first ballot will have been canceled so it cannot be used and would be caught if submitted. A photo of someone with two ballots on social media does not mean they can vote twice or that the system is broken. Voting twice or attempting to vote twice is illegal.

questions.q: What does it mean to “opt-out”?
questions.a: When you ‘opt-out’ of receiving a mail ballot, you are stating that you do not want to receive a mail ballot. Your county Clerk/ Registrar will then ensure that your name is not on the list of those active registered voters who will receive a mail ballot. When the Clerk/Registrar is ready to order or print ballots, your ballot will not be created.

questions.q: May I opt-out now?
questions.a: Yes, you may submit the ‘opt-out’ form now, but there is a deadline to submit prior to before each Election. If you submit an ‘opt-out’ form 60 days prior to any Election, you will NOT receive a mail ballot for the Presidential Preference Primary, the Primary or General Election, or any future elections.

questions.q: What happens if I get a ballot and then want to change my party affiliation?
questions.a: You are still able to change your party affiliation. Once you change your party affiliation (either online at VOTE.NV.gov (http://www.registertovote.nv.gov/), in person), your county Clerk/Registrar will automatically cancel the previous ballot, making it invalid, and will reissue you another ballot. The previous ballot will not work and if it is cast, the county Election Management System will recognize that it has been canceled as soon as the envelope is scanned, and it will prevent the ballot from being counted.

questions.q: Is there a way I can track my ballot?
questions.a: Yes, you can track your ballot online at MyBallot.NV.gov (https://myballot.nv.gov/login/Voter/Account/Login2?returnUrl=%2Flogin%2Fconnect%2Fauthorize%2Fcallback%3Fclient_id%3Dcore.voter.frontend%26scope%3Dopenid%2520profile%2520offline_access%26response_type%3Dcode%26redirect_uri%3Dhttps%253A%252F%252Fmyballot.nv.gov%252Fvoter%252Fapi%252Fauth%252Fcallback%26acr_values%3Dusertype%253AVoter%2520voterLoginMode%253Alight%2520shortName%253Anevada%26code_challenge%3DEuvkgfZL_ULsNfJiwNGIQX7BShqZR-8x767HEugwrD4%26code_challenge_method%3DS256).

questions.q: What is stopping someone from photocopying their ballot?
questions.a: Ballots are printed on special paper and use special bar codes that make each vote unique. A duplicate would be flagged in our voter management system and referred for investigation. It is illegal to vote or attempt to vote twice in an election.

questions.q: I heard third-party organizations are collecting ballots to turn them in. Are they safe?
questions.a:
We do not recommend the use of third-party organizations to return your ballot. This activity had previously been illegal, but the passage of Assembly Bill 321 made it legal to collect ballots for others. These organizations may be well intentioned, but they are not your county elections officials. Instead, we recommend you either return your ballot by mail or bring it to a secure drop-off location.

2026 Voting Locations - Early Voting and Election Day Locations and Drop Off locations. (https://www.nvsos.gov/elections/election-information/2026-election-information/2026-polling-locations)

questions.q: Should I trust the USPS (United States Postal Service)? Can they handle the volume of mail?
questions.a:
Yes, the USPS handles a tremendous volume of mail daily and the coming surge in elections related mail does not even begin to get close to their max capacity. For example, if everyone who gets a ballot mailed it in on the same day, this would still be less than 30% of their capacity.

Due to changes to pickup schedules at USPS, the Secretary of State's Office recommends mailing your ballot back at least a week before Election Day, or dropping it off at a polling location as it gets closer to Election Day.

questions.q: I made a mistake on my ballot? What can I do to fix it?
questions.a: If you mark the wrong candidate, you can cross out the candidate you mistakenly selected and mark the oval next to the correct candidate. Do not make an identifying mark next to the change, such as your initials, because that voids the ballot. In that instance, contact the election official in your county for assistance.

questions.q: How often will election night results be updated on your webpage?
questions.a: Election night results will be initially updated shortly after the close of polls and the last voter voting. After that, they will be updated routinely until the final update after the canvass of the vote by the respective Boards of County Commissioners/Board of Supervisors.

questions.q: When can I expect to start seeing election night results being reported?
questions.a: Once the Secretary of State has received confirmation from all the county clerks and registrars that the polls on election day are closed and all present voters in a polling location have cast their ballot (NAC 293.217(3)), results of the election will be posted. If a voter is in line at a polling location by 7pm local time, they will be allowed to vote.

questions.q: Where can I find election results from prior years?
questions.a: You may review prior years Elections results on our website here (https://www.nvsos.gov/elections/election-information/previous-elections/election-results). Hardcopies of election returns from any election may by obtained by contacting this office by phone or email.

questions.q: How can I get election results on election night?
questions.a: The Secretary of State's office provides election night results on our Silver State Elections (https://silverstateelection.nv.gov/) website.

questions.q: Does Nevada allow for write-in candidates?
questions.a: No, the State of Nevada does not allow individuals to write in a candidate’s name for any office. (NRS 293.270 (2))

questions.q: Is there a limit to the dollar amount of contributions I can accept as a candidate from one donor?
questions.a: Yes. The limit is $5,000 for the primary election and $5,000 for the general election, for a maximum of $10,000. If you receive more than $5,000 from any person and lose the primary election, you must return any amount in excess of $5,000 to the contributor (NRS 294A.100 and NRS 294A.160).

questions.q: What if I don’t have a primary election? Can I still receive the maximum of $10,000?
questions.a: Yes.

questions.q: Is there a limit to the dollar amount of contributions a Committee for Political Action (PAC) can receive from one donor?
questions.a: No. There is no limit to the dollar amount of contributions a PAC can receive or give to another PAC. However, PACs are still limited as to the amount they can contribute to an individual candidate (NRS 294A.100).

questions.q: What is an in-kind contribution?
questions.a: The value of goods or services provided in-kind for which money would have otherwise been paid (NRS 294A.007). For example, a person donates billboard space to a candidate free of charge. This would be an in-kind contribution, the value of which would be what it would normally cost to rent the billboard space.

questions.q: Can I make an anonymous contribution to a candidate?
questions.a: No. Anonymous contributions of $100 or more are prohibited (NRS 294A.190).

questions.q: Can I contribute to a candidate in the name of another person?
questions.a: No. Contributing in the name of another person, sometimes known as conduit or straw contributions, is prohibited by law (NRS 294A.122).

questions.q: Are the Contribution and Expense Reports (C&E Reports) the only finance forms I must file?
questions.a: No. If you receive more than $6,000 in annual compensation you must file a Financial Disclosure Statement (FDS) with the Secretary of State’s Office (NRS 281.561).

questions.q: What are Initiatives & Referenda Petitions?
questions.a:
Article 19 of the Constitution of the State of Nevada

A: Initiatives and referendums let Nevada citizens use petitions to have a direct say in laws. An initiative lets voters create new laws or change existing ones, including the state constitution. A referendum lets voters approve or reject laws that have already been passed. Both give voters a direct role in making decisions about laws.

questions.q: What is a Constitutional Initiative?
questions.a: Initiative Petitions (https://www.nvsos.gov/home/showpublisheddocument/18595) intend to Amend the Nevada State Constitution

questions.q: What is a Statutory Initiative?
questions.a: A statutory initiative seeks to create a new law or amend an existing state or local law.

questions.q: What is a Referendum?
questions.a: A referendum seeks to approve or disapprove an existing state or local law.

questions.q: How do I start a Constitutional, Statutory Initiative or Referendum Petition?
questions.a: Submit the Notice of Intent to Circulate a Petition (https://www.nvsos.gov/sos-information/forms-all-divisions/election-forms), and including the description of effect (https://www.nvsos.gov/sos-information/forms-all-divisions/election-forms) to the Secretary of States office on the prescribed form (https://www.nvsos.gov/home/showpublisheddocument/18599).

questions.q: Do I need to create a Political Action Committee before I circulate the petition for signatures?
questions.a: No, however if you intend on make contributions or expenditures designed to affect the outcome of a question on the ballot then you will need to submit a committee registration form (https://www.nvsos.gov/home/showpublisheddocument/16924/638997538740070000).

questions.q: How many signatures do I need to gather for a statewide petition?
questions.a: To get on the ballot, petitioners need signatures from registered voters equal to at least 10% (https://www.leg.state.nv.us/Const/NvConst.html#Art19) of those who voted in the last General Election. Only registered voters from the same county and petition district can sign.

questions.q: Can I get all the signatures in one County for a statewide petition?
questions.a: No, since you are attempting to amend the constitution or change and existing state law, you must collect signatures in each of the 4 Petition District in Nevada (https://www.leg.state.nv.us/nrs/NRS-295.html#NRS295Sec012).

questions.q: Where can I see what the 4 Petition Districts are?
questions.a: You can see Nevada’s 4 Congressional District Map on the Nevada Legislature website here (https://www.leg.state.nv.us/Division/Research/Districts/Reapp/2021/district-plans#districts-2011)

questions.q: Where can I get registered voter signatures for my petition?
questions.a: You can see a list of Designated Public Areas for Gathering of Signatures on Petitions on our website here (https://www.nvsos.gov/elections/initiatives-referenda/petition-district-maps/designation-of-public-areas-for-the-gathering-of-signatures-on-petitions)

questions.q: What is an independent candidate petition?
questions.a: An independent candidate petition is a document (https://www.nvsos.gov/home/showpublisheddocument/17582/639047786846270000) where people sign to support someone running for office without a political party, helping them qualify to appear on the ballot.

questions.q: What is a minor party petition?
questions.a: A minor party may qualify for ballot access if they submit a petition containing valid signatures equal to 1% (NRS 293.1715 (https://www.leg.state.nv.us/nrs/nrs-293.html#NRS293Sec1715)) of the total number of votes cast at the last preceding general election for the office of the Representative in Congress which must be apportions equally among petition districts.

questions.q: What is a Recall Petition NRS 306.015?
questions.a: A petition that is circulated with the intent to recall a public officer before their term ends. You can read about Recall Petitions here or NRS. 306.015 (https://www.leg.state.nv.us/nrs/nrs-306.html#NRS306Sec015)

questions.q: What is a PAC?
questions.a: A group that raises or spends money to influence elections, not including individuals, political parties, candidates’ own campaign committees, recall groups, or businesses/unions acting on their own. It also doesn’t include groups like lawmakers’ party organizations or businesses simply providing normal services NRS 294.0055 (https://www.leg.state.nv.us/NRS/NRS-294a.html#NRS294ASec0055)

questions.q: Are there different types of PAC’s?
questions.a: Yes, there is a Committee for Political Action(PAC), Committee Sponsored by a Political Party, Recall Committee, Committee for Political Action (PAC) Advocating Passage & Non-Profit Operating as a Political Action Committee per NRS 294.0055 (https://www.leg.state.nv.us/NRS/NRS-294a.html#NRS294ASec0055)

questions.q: If I am out of the State of Nevada, can I form a PAC in Nevada?
questions.a: Yes, however all PAC’s need to list a Registered agent on the prescribed form (https://www.nvsos.gov/home/showpublisheddocument/16924/638997538740070000). The registered Agent must have a Nevada address that is available for service of process during business hours.

questions.q: If I am already registered as a Federal PAC do I have to register as a Nevada PAC?
questions.a: Yes, if you contribute more than $5000 in a calendar year with the purpose of affecting the outcome of any election

questions.q: Do I need to start a PAC if I am a political candidate?
questions.a: No, candidates are not required (https://www.leg.state.nv.us/NRS/NRS-294a.html#NRS294ASec130) to establish or register a separate campaign committee for the purpose of reporting contributions and expenses (https://www.leg.state.nv.us/NRS/NRS-294a.html#NRS294ASec120).

questions.q: How long does someone have to be in the office before they can be recalled?
questions.a: A six months wait only applies to those who are not a Senator or Assemblyman/woman in the legislature. For those in the legislature, the petition can be filed starting on Feb 11, 2027 since the session starts on Feb 1, 2027 (84th session)and the NV Constitution states, “No such petition shall be circulated or filed against any officer until he has actually held his office six (6) months, save and except that it may be filed against a senator or assemblyman in the legislature at any time after ten (10) days from the beginning of the first session after his election”.

questions.q: Can anyone file a petition for recall?
questions.a:
There are some limitations to who can file it. NRS 306.015 (https://www.leg.state.nv.us/nrs/nrs-306.html#NRS306Sec015) states that the Notice of Intent must be filed by those proposing to circulate the petition, (up to three people), who must meet the qualifications of 306.015 including that they must have voted in the election at which the person they are seeking to recall was elected.

Some states have limitations on recalling elections for ethical or legal violations, but Nevada does not. It isn’t up to us (in other words) to state if it is a “good or bad reason”. The requirement is that the petition must have a 200-word description: “They shall set forth in said petition, in not exceeding two hundred (200) words, the reasons why said recall is demanded.”

questions.q: Does it go to a Special Election?
questions.a: Yes, if the petition is filed (and has enough validated signatures) then it must go to a special election within 30 days.

questions.q: Who can demand a recount?
questions.a:
Pursuant to NRS 293.403(1) (https://www.leg.state.nv.us/nrs/nrs-293.html#NRS293Sec403), a candidate that was defeated at any election may demand and receive a recount of the vote for office for which he or she is a candidate to determine the number of votes received for the candidate and the number of votes received for the person who won the election.

NRS 293.403(2) (https://www.leg.state.nv.us/nrs/nrs-293.html#NRS293Sec403) states that any voter can demand a recount for a ballot question within 3 working days after the canvass of the vote and the certification.

questions.q: When does the canvass occur?
questions.a:
According to NRS 293.387 (https://www.leg.state.nv.us/nrs/nrs-293.html#NRS293Sec387), for county offices, the Board of County Commissioners must canvass not later than the 10th day after the Election Day.

For statewide and multi-county offices and ballot questions, NRS 293.395 (https://www.leg.state.nv.us/nrs/nrs-293.html#NRS293Sec395) requires the Nevada Supreme Court to canvass on the fourth Tuesday of November after each general election.

questions.q: When does a request for a recount need to be submitted?
questions.a: Within 3 working days after the canvass of the vote.

questions.q: What do I need to submit as a candidate who demands a recount?
questions.a:
The candidate who demands the recount will file a written demand with the officer with whom the candidate filed his or her declaration of candidacy and deposits in advance the estimated costs of the recount with that officer. It does not need to be on a specific form.

The payment must be cash, certified check, or money order, and not a personal check.

questions.q: What is included in the cost estimates for the recount?
questions.a: NAC 293.375 (https://www.leg.state.nv.us/nac/NAC-293.html#NAC293Sec375) provides details regarding what is used to determine each county estimate for the cost of a recount.

questions.q: When does the recount process start after the demand has been made?
questions.a: The recount must start within five days of receiving the demand and must be completed within 5 days once it has commenced.

questions.q: If I demand a recount, can I withdraw that demand?
questions.a:
Yes. NAC 293.371 (https://www.leg.state.nv.us/nac/NAC-293.html#NAC293Sec371) clarifies that a person who demands a recount of votes may withdraw the demand by filing a withdrawal in writing with the officer with whom the person filed the demand at any time before the completion of the recount.

If that occurs, each county or city clerk who was conducting the recount must stop the recount as soon as practicable after the person demanding the recount files the withdrawal of the demand. A person who withdraws a demand for a recount of votes may not request a continuation of the recount or a new recount of those votes.

questions.q: Would someone have to pay if they demand a recount and then withdraw it?
questions.a:
Yes. If a person files a withdrawal of a demand for a recount, each county or city clerk who was conducting the recount must determine the actual cost incurred before the withdrawal was filed. If the sum deposited for the purpose of the recount:

(a) Is less than the cost of the recount at the time of the withdrawal, the person shall, upon demand, pay the deficiency to the county clerk, city clerk or Secretary of State, as applicable.

(b) Is in excess of the cost of the recount at the time of the withdrawal, the excess must be refunded to the person.

questions.q: Has there ever been widespread voter fraud in a Nevada election?
questions.a: No. We use complex systems and checks and balances to ensure widespread fraud does not happen. Every unique situation that appears to be a violation of any state or federal election law is investigated thoroughly. Information about election investigations can be found here. (https://www.nvsos.gov/Admin/Components/FAQ/FAQ/Edit/?navid=2923)

questions.q: Has there ever been widespread voter fraud in a Nevada election?
questions.a: No. We use complex systems and checks and balances to ensure widespread fraud does not happen. Every unique situation that appears to be a violation of any state or federal election law is investigated thoroughly. Information about election investigations can be found here. (https://www.nvsos.gov/elections/election-information/election-investigations)

questions.q: What is voter intimidation?
questions.a: Voter intimidation includes several actions, including interfering with voters at the polls. It is currently illegal under NRS 293.2543 (https://www.leg.state.nv.us/Division/Legal/LawLibrary/NRS/NRS-293.html#NRS293Sec2543) through NRS 293.2549 (https://www.leg.state.nv.us/Division/Legal/LawLibrary/NRS/NRS-293.html#NRS293Sec2549) and under federal laws.

questions.q: Who do I tell if I feel that I’ve been a victim of voter intimidation or other elections-related crime?
questions.a:
If it was an act of violence, call 911.

For any other election-related crimes, contact our office at this number (775) 687-8683 and we will notify the Elections Integrity Task Force (EITF) who will take appropriate action. Additionally, we request you fill out an Elections Integrity Violation Report (EIVR) so that we can formally track and address the issue. They are located online at this site: Report Potential Election Law Violation in Nevada (https://www.nvsos.gov/Admin/Components/FAQ/FAQ/Edit/?navid=256)

questions.q: What is an EIVR (Election Integrity Violation Report)?
questions.a: An Elections Integrity Violation Report is a simple written report notifying this office about a violation of Title 24 Election Law (Nevada Revised Statutes). It is not a police report. If you want to report an act of violence, please call 911. To file an EIVR, you can find the document at: Election Integrity Violation Report (https://www.nvsos.gov/home/showpublisheddocument/4281/638113631420500000)

questions.q: May I submit an EIVR anonymously?
questions.a: No, you cannot submit one anonymously. It is important that we can follow up with you about the complaint to get additional details, documentation, pictures, or information that you may have.

questions.q: Does same-day registration enable voter fraud?
questions.a: No. There are many measures in place to prevent and identify attempted voter fraud within the same-day registration process. To same-day register a voter must have a valid Nevada driver’s license or Nevada ID card and must present it to the election official at their polling place; this prevents non-Nevada residents from fraudulently utilizing the same-day registration process. In addition, before the same-day registration provisional ballots are counted, a statewide report is run that compares the names and driver’s license/ID card numbers of all provisional voters to ensure only one ballot will be counted per voter. This report also compares all provisional voters to all the in-person and by-mail voters whose ballots were already counted to ensure provisional voters have not already voted. Voters who commit voter fraud are guilty of a category D felony and are prosecuted to the full extent of the law. Even attempting to vote more than once in the same election is voter fraud.

questions.q: What are some of the things I can do to prepare myself for working at a polling location?
questions.a:
- Be prepared for a long day. Get plenty of rest and wear comfortable shoes and clothes. Dress in layers in case it is cold in the facility. Wear something patriotic, but leave any clothing, stickers, etc., supporting a political candidate, issue, or organization.
- Pack what you need for the full day. Make sure you have plenty of food, drinks, and any other items to sustain you throughout the day.
- Know your job duties. Be prepared as possible by completing poll worker training, review any training materials that have been provided to you, and ask questions before and during the day if you’re unsure of how to handle something.
- We know it will be a long day and working with a new group of people can be tough. Having a great attitude and spreading good vibes can help keep morale high.
- As an election worker your job is to make sure every eligible voter can cast a ballot, no matter who they’re voting for. Make sure every voter feels safe and welcome at your polling location.
- Make every voter’s experience a positive and empowering one. As an election worker, you can help shape their experience, create positive memories of voting, and make lifelong voters out of everyone you meet.

questions.q: Who is eligible to be an election worker?
questions.a:
- Must be a registered voter in the State of Nevada.
- Must not be a candidate or a member of a candidate’s immediate family.
- Must be at least 18 years of age or;
- 16- and 17-year-olds may serve as a student election worker.

If you are interested in being an election worker, click here to complete the “Election Worker Interest Form (https://app.smartsheetgov.com/b/form/99c5115c05d145b0a843781140593524)”.

questions.q: How do I submit a public records request?
questions.a:
Our office is committed to providing access to public records in accordance with NRS 239. All requests to inspect and/or obtain copies of public records mist be made through the office of the Public Information Officer at sosrecords@sos.nv.gov (mailto:sospio@sos.nv.gov) or your request can be mailed to Public Information Officer, Nevada Secretary of State, 101 North Carson Street, Ste 3, Carson City, NV 89701.

The form you will need to complete is below:

Public Record Request Pursuant to NRS 239 (nvsos.gov) (https://www.nvsos.gov/home/showpublisheddocument/2785/638086087489670000)

For additional information about the public records request process, click on the link below:

Public Records Requests | Nevada Secretary of State (nvsos.gov) (https://www.nvsos.gov/Admin/Components/FAQ/FAQ/Edit/?navid=1307)

questions.q: WHO IS ELIGIBLE TO VOTE BY MAIL?
questions.a: In Nevada, all active registered voters will be mailed a vote-by-mail ballot as long as they are registered no later than 14 days before Election Day.

questions.q: HOW CAN I RETURN MY BALLOT BY MAIL?
questions.a:
Voted ballots sent through the mail must be:

(1) Mailed in the postage-paid return envelope provided specifically for you, showing your name and address, and you must also sign the outside of that envelope before mailing it;

(2) Postmarked on or before Election Day; and

(3) Received by the Election Department by 5 pm on the fourth day after Election Day if postmarked, or by 5 pm on the third day after Election Day if not postmarked.

Do not put your ballot in another voter’s return envelope.

questions.q: WHAT IS THE DEADLINE TO SUBMIT MY MAIL BALLOT?
questions.a: Your mail ballot must be postmarked by Election Day and received by 5 p.m. on the fourth day after Election Day. If your ballot is not postmarked, it must be received by 5 p.m. on the third day after Election Day. Ballots can also be hand-delivered in person by 7 p.m. on Election Day.

questions.q: CAN I VOTE IN PERSON EVEN IF I HAVE RECEIVED A VOTE-BY-MAIL BALLOT?
questions.a:
As long as you haven’t returned your voted ballot, you can vote in person. In order to vote in person, you must surrender your vote-by-mail ballot or sign a form affirming that you have not voted your ballot and will not attempt to vote twice. You may also "opt-out" of receiving future ballots by mail by submitting the appropriate form.

You have two options for voting in person:

Early Voting: Early voting begins 17 days before the election and ends 4 days before the election. Days and hours of operation vary by county. A list of early voting polling places by county can be found here (https://www.nvsos.gov/sos/elections/voters/early-voting-information). In order to avoid lines on Election Day, all voters who wish to vote in person are encouraged to vote early.

Election Day: Polling locations open at 7am on Election Day and remain open until 7pm. As long as you are in line by 7pm, you will be allowed to vote. A list of Election Day polling places by county can be found here (https://www.nvsos.gov/sos/elections/election-information).

questions.q: WHEN ARE BALLOTS MAILED TO ACTIVE REGISTERED VOTERS?
questions.a: Ballots are mailed starting no later than 20 days before Election Day for in-state voters and no later than 40-45 days before Election Day for out-of-state voters. If you don’t receive your mail ballot packet by the start of early voting, immediately contact your local election office (https://absentee.vote411.org/vote/eoddomestic.htm).

questions.q: HOW CAN I CHECK IF I AM AN INACTIVE VOTER?
questions.a: You can check your voter registration status on the secretary of state’s website (https://registertovote.nv.gov/).

questions.q: HOW CAN I TRACK MY MAILED BALLOT?
questions.a: You can sign up to track your mail ballot using your secretary of state’s resource (https://www.nvsos.gov/votersearch/). If you have any issues with your state’s online tracker, please contact your local election office (https://absentee.vote411.org/vote/eoddomestic.htm).

questions.q: HOW DO I OPT-OUT OF GETTING A MAIL BALLOT?
questions.a: To opt-out, you must submit a written or online request to not receive a mail ballot by 60 days before Election Day. You can opt-out online (https://www.nvsos.gov/votersearch/) or by mail. To opt-out by mail, you can print, complete, and mail a Mail Ballot Preference Form (https://www.nvsos.gov/sos/home/showpublisheddocument/13305/638478223678570000).

questions.q: HOW DO I REQUEST AN EMERGENCY ABSENTEE BALLOT?
questions.a:
Nevada has an emergency absentee voting program. An absentee ballot can be brought to you at a hospital or other medical facility in certain emergency circumstances. Requests for an emergency absentee ballot must be made in writing and submitted any time before 5:00 p.m. on the day of the election.

Such requests must be due to an illness or disability resulting in confinement to a medical facility, including nursing homes, sudden hospitalization, serious illness, or being called away from home after the deadline for requesting a standard absentee ballot. Please contact your local election office (https://absentee.vote411.org/vote/eoddomestic.htm) for more information.

questions.q: I’M VOTING FOR THE FIRST TIME BY MAIL. WHAT SHOULD I KNOW?
questions.a:
If you are a first time voter, you may be required to present ID for voting if: (a) The data you provided on your voter registration application didn’t match the data on file at the Department of Motor Vehicles or Social Security Administration; and (b) You didn’t respond to the letter that was sent to you notifying you of the discrepancy.

Your county clerk will notify you if you are required to provide a copy of your identification with your mail ballot. To fulfill this requirement, you must submit both identity and residency identification with your mail ballot.

"Official Identification" means a government-issued, or otherwise official, article or combination of articles, which establishes both the identity and residence.

Forms of ID may include:

- A current and valid Nevada driver's license
- A current and valid identification card issued by the Department of Motor Vehicles
- A current and valid identification card issued by a branch of the Armed Forces of the United States
- A current and valid identification card issued by a sheriff of a Nevada county to an employee as a condition of employment by certain business enterprises
- A current and valid identification card issued by an agency of the State of Nevada or political subdivision thereof or the United States, including, without limitation, a public school, college or university
- Current and valid student identification card from an accredited private school, college or university
- Current and valid United States passport
- Current and valid insurance plan identification card which the county clerk determines, in his or her discretion, to be a reliable indication of the true name and identity of the person
- Current and valid tribal identification card

Proof of residency may include:

- Any form of ID set forth above
- Current and valid utility bill, including, without limitation, a bill for electricity, gas, oil, water, sewer, septic, telephone, cellular telephone or cable television
- Current and valid bank or credit union statement
- Current and valid paycheck
- Current and valid income tax return
- Current and valid statement concerning mortgage, rental or lease of a residence
- Current and valid motor vehicle registration
- Current and valid document issued by a governmental agency
- Current and valid property tax statement
- Any other official article which the county clerk determines, in his or her discretion, to be a reliable indication of the true residential address of the person

If you have questions on this process, please contact your local election office (https://absentee.vote411.org/vote/eoddomestic.htm).

questions.q: WHAT IS THE DEADLINE FOR CURING MY MAIL BALLOT SIGNATURE IF THERE’S AN ISSUE?
questions.a: If a question arises about your signature on the outside of your mail ballot return envelope or if you did not put your signature on the outside of that envelope, the Election Department will notify you using the contact information in your voter registration. You will have until 5pm on the sixth day after Election Day to provide a signature confirmation or an actual signature, as applicable.

questions.q: HOW DO I RECEIVE A BALLOT BY MAIL AS AN OVERSEAS OR U.S. MILITARY VOTER?
questions.a:
Overseas citizens and U.S. military personnel can find information on how to register to vote and request an absentee ballot at the Overseas Vote Foundation (https://www.overseasvotefoundation.org/vote/home.htm).

  Request your Ballot  (https://absentee.vote411.org/vote/VoterInformation.htm)

questions.q: Does Nevada allow ballot curing?
questions.a: Yes, Nevada allows voters to fix an issue with their ballot.

questions.q: How will I know if there’s an issue with my absentee or mail-in ballot?
questions.a: The county clerk’s office will contact you via letter, phone, or email if any errors are found.

questions.q: How do I cure my ballot?
questions.a: The notice from your county clerk’s office will include the necessary information and instructions to correct (cure) your ballot on time.

questions.q: What is the deadline to cure my ballot?
questions.a: The deadline to cure (correct) your absentee/mail ballot is by 5pm on the 6th day after the election.

questions.q: Can I track the status of my ballot online after curing it?
questions.a: You can track your ballot through your state’s online tool. (https://nevada.ballottrax.net/voter/)

questions.q: What is a ballot drop box?
questions.a: A drop box is a secure, locked structure operated by election officials where voters can deliver their absentee ballot any time, day or night.

questions.q: Are drop boxes available in my state?
questions.a: Yes, vote-by-mail drop boxes are available in Nevada.

questions.q: Where can I find ballot drop box locations?
questions.a: Ballot drop-off locations are available here.  (https://www.nvsos.gov/elections/election-information/2026-election-information)

questions.q: Can I track the ballot after placing in the drop box?
questions.a: Yes, you can track your ballot by looking up your on the Secretary of State website. (https://nevada.ballottrax.net/voter/)

questions.q: Can I vote before Election Day in Nevada?
questions.a: Yes. Nevada offers early in-person voting, and all active registered voters are also mailed a ballot. You can choose to vote early in person, vote by mail, or vote on Election Day.

questions.q: Who can vote early in Nevada?
questions.a: Any registered voter can vote early at an early voting location in their county. You do not need to apply to vote early.

questions.q: When can I vote early in Nevada?
questions.a: Early voting in Nevada typically begins 17 days before Election Day and ends 4 days before Election Day. Be sure to check the exact dates for your election.

questions.q: Where can I vote early in Nevada?
questions.a:
You can vote at any early voting location in your county. Hours and locations vary, so be sure to check your county’s (https://absentee.vote411.org/vote/eoddomestic.htm) schedule before you go.

All active registered voters in Nevada are mailed a ballot. If you prefer, you can complete and return your mail ballot instead of voting early in person.

questions.q: Who is eligible to vote in Nevada?
questions.a:
To register and vote in Nevada, you must:

- Be a U.S. citizen
- Be at least 18 years old on or before Election Day (you can preregister at 17)
- Be a resident of Nevada and your county for at least 30 days before the election
- Not be currently serving a term of imprisonment for a felony conviction
- Not have been declared mentally incompetent by a court

questions.q: Can I vote in Nevada if I have a felony conviction?
questions.a: In Nevada, you only lose your right to vote if you are currently incarcerated for a felony conviction. If you lost your voting rights because of a conviction, you could register to vote immediately after release. Your voting rights are not restricted by pretrial detention, misdemeanors, probation, or parole.

questions.q: How do I vote in Nevada if I don’t have a permanent address?
questions.a: You can still register to vote in Nevada. A description must be provided if you reside at a location that has not been assigned a street address. This can be a description of a street corner, park, shelter, or any other place where you usually stay. The mailing address on your registration form can be a PO box, local shelter, advocacy organization, outreach center, or the home of someone who will accept mail for you.

questions.q: Can students vote in Nevada?
questions.a:
Yes. Students can register and vote in Nevada using their school or campus address if they consider it their residence.

If you move, such as to a different dorm or off campus, be sure to update your voter registration so you vote in the correct district.

If you are a student from out of state, you can also choose to vote in your home state using an absentee ballot, but you’ll need to follow your home state’s rules and deadlines. You can find the rules for your state on VOTE411 or by contacting your state’s election office (https://absentee.vote411.org/vote/eoddomestic.htm).

questions.q: Do I need an ID to register to vote in Nevada?
questions.a: Yes, you need a valid photo ID to register to vote in Nevada. If you do not have one when you register, you must show it at your polling place on Election Day.

questions.q: What types of ID are accepted for registration?
questions.a:
The ID should prove where you live, verify your identity, and include a photo.

- For online registration (https://www.nvsos.gov/SOSVoterServices/start.aspx), you will need a DMV-issued Driver's License or ID.
- If you're using a paper registration form, (https://www.nvsos.gov/sosvoterregform/) you'll need to provide either a valid NV Driver’s License or ID Card number or the last 4 digits of your Social Security Number. If you don't have any of these, your County Election Department will contact you after receiving your application.

If you wish to register on the same day as the election, you will need to have a valid Nevada driver’s license or ID card, and you must vote in person at a polling location. Tribal ID cards may also work if they meet specific requirements (https://www.nvsos.gov/sos/elections/election-information/same-day-registration). Other forms of identification, like military IDs or passports, cannot be used for same-day registration.

If your current photo ID doesn't have your current address, bring a copy of a current utility bill, bank statement, government check, or another government document showing your name and current address.

questions.q: What if I don’t have an ID?
questions.a:
If you do not have the above ID when you register, you will need to provide it before you vote either in person or by mail.

Voters can call or text 844-338-8743 at any time to reach VoteRiders Voter ID Helpline

questions.q: When are official election results available in Nevada?
questions.a: Official results are never available on Election Day. Election officials are working around the clock to count a large number of ballots, and it’s essential that they take the time to make sure every vote is counted.

questions.q: Where can I find official election results?
questions.a:
Official election results will be uploaded on the Nevada Secretary of State’s website (https://www.nvsos.gov/sos/elections/election-information/precinct-level-results) as they become available.

  Official Results  (https://www.nvsos.gov/sos/elections/election-information/precinct-level-results)

questions.q: What does a poll worker do in Nevada?
questions.a: Poll workers in Nevada help run elections at voting locations. They assist with setting up and closing the polling place, checking in voters, issuing ballots, answering questions, and making sure the voting process runs smoothly and securely.

questions.q: What qualifications do I need to be a poll worker in Nevada?
questions.a:
To be a poll worker in Nevada, you must:

- Be registered to vote in Nevada
- Be at least 18 years old, or at least 16 years old and enrolled in high school
- Not be a candidate for nomination or election, or closely related to a candidate
- Not be a candidate for nomination or election, or closely related to a candidate

questions.q: Are poll workers paid in Nevada?
questions.a: Yes, poll workers in Nevada are compensated for their time. Pay varies by county and position. Some counties may also offer mileage or expense reimbursement. Contact your county election office (https://absentee.vote411.org/vote/eoddomestic.htm) for specific pay rates.

questions.q: How do I apply to be a poll worker in Nevada?
questions.a: You can apply to be a poll worker by contacting your county election office (https://absentee.vote411.org/vote/eoddomestic.htm) or visiting your county’s election website (https://www.nvsos.gov/elections/poll-workers). Each county manages its own poll worker recruitment and application process.

questions.q: What is a provisional ballot?
questions.a: Provisional ballots ensure that all voters can cast a ballot even if voter eligibility isn’t certain when they vote. Voters can mark a provisional ballot, and election workers set it aside until eligibility is verified at a later time.

questions.q: Does Nevada offer provisional voting?
questions.a: Yes, Nevada offers provisional voting.

questions.q: Can I vote a provisional ballot?
questions.a:
You are eligible to vote a provisional ballot if:

- You claim to be an eligible voter, but your name does not appear on the list of registered voters, and the voter registrar cannot determine your registration.
- You have applied for a ballot by mail but have not returned it or canceled it.
- You vote during extended polling hours ordered by a state or federal court.
- You do not present any acceptable form of identification.

questions.q: How can I check the status of my provisional ballot?
questions.a: If you voted a provisional ballot, you can check its status (https://www.nvsos.gov/sos/elections/voters/provisional-voting) using the special affirmation number given to you at your polling place. You can call (877) 766-8683 or use the Provisional Ballot Status link to find your affirmation number. You can start checking your Provisional Ballot Status on the 8th day following the election, and it remains available for 30 days.

questions.q: What voting assistance is available for voters with disabilities?
questions.a:
The Help America Vote Act requires that election authorities have voting equipment for voters with disabilities to vote privately and independently, and Nevada is no exception.

Nevada's Effective Absentee System for Elections, or EASE (https://www.nvsos.gov/ease/easepages/overview.aspx), is available to Nevada residents with disabilities. EASE is an online tool that combines voter registration, electronic ballot delivery, and marking.

You can also contact your local election official for more information or assistance.

You have the right to bring an interpreter with you to the polls or to get language assistance from anyone you choose, including a poll worker, as long as the person is not your employer, an agent of your employer, or an officer or agent of your labor union.

For more information on the provisions available for disabled voters, please contact your local election authority (https://absentee.vote411.org/vote/eoddomestic.htm).

questions.q: How do I request accommodation or report accessibility issues?
questions.a: If you have any questions about receiving help in voting, please ask the clerk or inspector at the polling place.

questions.q: Can I vote by mail because of my disability?
questions.a:
Vote-by-mail (absentee voting) is available in Nevada and no excuse is required. You can find more about how to vote by mail here. (https://www.vote411.org/nevada#absentee-ballot-process)

For more information, you can utilize the American Association of People With Disabilities (AAPD) (http://www.aapd.com/what-we-do/voting/) resource.

questions.q: Does Nevada require employers to give time off to vote?
questions.a:
Yes. Nevada law requires employers to provide paid time off to vote if an employee does not have sufficient time outside of working hours to vote.

Employees can receive:

- Up to 1 hour if the polling place is within 2 miles
- Up to 2 hours if it is 2–10 miles away
- Up to 3 hours if it is more than 10 miles away

Employees must request time off before Election Day, and employers may specify the hours the employee can be absent.

questions.q: Do I need ID to vote in Nevada?
questions.a:
Nevada does not require most voters to show ID when voting in person because you must verify your identity when you register to vote.

If you are a first-time voter, and did not provide an acceptable form of ID with your registration from, you may be asked to show ID at the polls

questions.q: What types of ID can I use to vote in-person in Nevada?
questions.a:
If you are asked to show ID, you can use a document that includes your name and address, such as a current:

- Nevada driver’s license or state ID
- U.S. passport
- Military ID
- Tribal ID
- Government-issued ID

If your ID does not have your current address, you also need to provide a document showing your name and current address to prove your residency. You can use:

- A utility bill, bank statement, paycheck, or other government document with your name and address

questions.q: Do I need ID to vote by mail/absentee in Nevada?
questions.a:
Most voters do not need to provide ID when voting by mail. Your signature is used to verify your identity.

If you are a first-time voter who registered by mail and did not provide ID when registering, you may need to include a copy of an acceptable ID (https://www.nvsos.gov/sos/elections/voters/mail-ballot-voting) with your ballot.

questions.q: What if I don’t have an acceptable ID?
questions.a:
If you are voting in person and cannot provide ID when requested, you may be able to vote using a provisional ballot [link to provisional voting state topic]. Your election officials will provide instructions on what steps are needed for your ballot to be counted.

If you are voting by mail, your signature will typically be used to verify your identity. If there is an issue with your signature, you will be contacted and given an opportunity to correct it.

questions.q: Are student or digital IDs accepted?
questions.a:
Because Nevada does not generally require ID to vote in person, student or digital IDs are not typically needed.

If ID is requested, it must show your name and address. Some student or digital IDs may not meet these requirements, so it’s best to use a government-issued ID or another accepted document if available.

questions.q: What is the deadline to register to vote in Nevada?
questions.a:
- Online registration deadline: 5 days before Election Day
- Register by mail deadline: Postmarked 28 days before Election Day
- In-person registration deadline: Election Day

Deadlines for special elections may be different. Please contact your local elections official for these deadlines.

questions.q: How can I check my voter registration status?
questions.a: You can verify your voter registration status using Nevada’s voter information tool. (https://www.nvsos.gov/votersearch/)

questions.q: Does Nevada have online voter registration?
questions.a: Yes! Use our online registration tool (https://www.vote411.org/register) to complete your application.

questions.q: Is same-day voter registration available in Nevada?
questions.a: Yes, you can register in person on Election Day. If you would like to register to vote on the same day as the election, you must have a valid Nevada driver’s license or ID card. There are no exceptions to this requirement.

questions.q: Can I pre-register to vote?
questions.a: Yes, you can pre-register at 17 years old.

questions.q: Who is eligible to register in Nevada?
questions.a: Check if you’re eligible to register here (https://www.vote411.org/nevada#eligibility-requirements).

questions.q: How do I update my voter registration?
questions.a:
If you moved within the state of Nevada, changed your name, or want to switch your political party affiliation, you will need to fill out a new form to update your voter registration. To do this, go to RegisterToVote.NV.gov (http://registertovote.nv.gov/).

If you moved to another state and need to cancel your Nevada voter registration, you can do so using the state’s online cancellation tool (https://www.nvsos.gov/SOSVoterServices/cancel/CancelStep0.aspx).

questions.q: What types of voting machines does Nevada use?
questions.a: The voting system used in Nevada is Direct Recording Electronic (DRE).

questions.q: What is Direct Recording Electronic Voting?
questions.a:
Direct Recording Electronic (DRE) is the newest system in use in the U.S. All the information about who and what you are voting for is on an electronic screen like a TV or computer screen.

There are many variations of DREs because many companies are inventing new ones, and many cities, counties, and states are trying them out.

- Usually, after you have signed in, the poll workers will give you a card that you slide into a device to start your voting session.
- Some of these devices will show all candidates and ballot choices on one big screen. Often, with these big screen devices you push a button next to the name of the candidate you want to vote for (or yes or no on a ballot measure).
- On other DREs, the screen is set up to show pages. There will probably be one thing on which to vote on each screen or page. For example, on one screen or page, you might vote for the president. Then you might move to the next page to vote for a senator. Often these small-screen devices have a touch screen, where you touch the screen next to the name of the person you want to vote for.
- Other devices have a keypad, and some have a keyboard, so you can write in the name of someone you want to vote for.
- You let the system know you are finished voting by pushing a button, touching the screen or entering something on a keypad.

You can learn more about voting systems by checking out the Elections Assistance Commission's (EAC) resource.  (https://www.eac.gov/voting-equipment/system-certification-process)

questions.q: Campaign Finance Information
questions.a:
For information on federal campaign contributions, please visit Open Secrets (http://www.opensecrets.org).

For information on state campaign contributions, please visit your state's resource. (http://nvsos.gov/sos/elections/candidate-information/campaign-finance-reporting-requirements)

questions.q: Candidate and Ballot Measure Information
questions.a: Information on local, state and federal candidates and ballot measures may be available here (https://www.vote411.org/ballot#.UFoDEFHh-Sp).

questions.q: Election Dates
questions.a:
The next election dates can be found here www.VOTE411.org/nevada (https://www.VOTE411.org/nevada).

Contact your local Board of Elections (https://absentee.vote411.org/vote/eoddomestic.htm) for more information.

questions.q: Election Day Voting Hours
questions.a: Polling place hours of operation are from 7:00 am to 7:00 pm.

questions.q: Overseas and Military Voters
questions.a:
You are a Military or Overseas voter if you are in uniformed services, living overseas OR a spouse or dependent of a uniformed services voter. To get registered and vote, you can utilize Overseas Vote Foundation. (https://voterhelpdesk.usvotefoundation.org/en/support/home)

If you have additional questions about elections and voting overseas you can use our state specific elections official directory or contact the Overseas Vote Foundation. (https://voterhelpdesk.usvotefoundation.org/en/support/home)

questions.q: Polling Place Locations
questions.a: You can find your polling place by utilizing your state resource (https://www.nvsos.gov/elections/election-information/2026-election-information/2026-polling-locations). If you have further questions on your polling place location, please contact your county clerk. (https://absentee.vote411.org/vote/eoddomestic.htm)

questions.q: Primary Election Process
questions.a:
Nevada is a “closed primary” state. In order to vote in the primary election, voters must be registered with a political party. Unaffiliated or independent voters are not able to participate in the primary.

If you have any questions about your state’s primary election, please contact your local election officials (https://absentee.vote411.org/vote/eoddomestic.htm).

questions.q: Verify Voter Registration
questions.a:
To verify your registration status

  click here!  (https://nvsos.gov/votersearch/Index.aspx)

questions.q: Vote by Mail
questions.a:
Nevada is now a vote by mail state, so all registered voters will receive a ballot by mail. You may opt-out from receiving a mail-in ballot if you wish to vote in person. Do not mail a ballot and vote in person. Voters who vote in person will have two options:

1. Early Voting - Early voting begins on 17 days before the election and ends 4 days before the election. Days and hours of operation vary by county. A list of early voting polling places by county can be found here (https://www.nvsos.gov/sos/elections/election-day-information). In order to avoid lines on Election Day, all voters who wish to vote in person are encouraged to vote early.
2. Election Day - Polling locations open at 7:00 am on Election Day and remain open until 7:00 pm. As long as you are in line by 7:00 pm, you will be allowed to vote. A list of Election Day polling places by county can be found here (https://www.nvsos.gov/sos/elections/election-day-information).
